name: Shadow Credentials (msDS-KeyCredentialLink Abuse)
description: Abuses write access (GenericWrite / GenericAll / WriteProperty) over a target's msDS-KeyCredentialLink attribute to add an attacker-controlled key credential, then authenticates via PKINIT to recover the target's TGT and NT hash - no password reset required, so it is stealthier and reversible. Core of the HTB Fluffy chain (winrm_svc and ca_svc takeover).
source: HTB Fluffy engagement; The Hacker Recipes - Shadow Credentials
notes:
=== WHY SHADOW CREDENTIALS WORKS ===
Any principal with write access to a target's msDS-KeyCredentialLink attribute
(GenericWrite, GenericAll, WriteProperty, or explicit write on that attribute) can
add a Key Credential - a raw public key used for PKINIT (certificate-based Kerberos
pre-auth). Once the key is planted, you request a TGT via PKINIT using the matching
private key, then UnPAC-the-hash to recover the target's NT hash.

=== WHY IT IS PREFERRED OVER FORCECHANGEPASSWORD ===
  - No password reset: the target account keeps working, so it does not break
    services or alert the owner (ForceChangePassword is LOUD and disruptive).
  - Reversible: remove the key credential afterward (certipy shadow ... does this).
  - Yields both a TGT and the NT hash in one shot.

=== REQUIREMENTS ===
  - Write over target msDS-KeyCredentialLink (from BloodHound: AddKeyCredentialLink edge).
  - A DC with a Domain Controller certificate (PKINIT enabled) - true in almost every AD CS / default DC.
  - Clock in sync with the DC (see ad-faketime-kerberos) or PKINIT fails with KRB_AP_ERR_SKEW.

=== FLUFFY CHAIN POSITION ===
  p.agila (GenericAll on service accounts) -> Shadow Creds on winrm_svc -> user flag
  -> Shadow Creds on ca_svc -> ESC16 UPN spoof -> Administrator.

=== OUTPUT ===
  certipy prints: [*] NT hash for '<target_account>': aad3b435...:<nthash>
  Use that hash for pass-the-hash / evil-winrm / further enumeration.

defense.why_it_works: A principal with write access to the target's msDS-KeyCredentialLink attribute plants an attacker-owned key credential; the DC then accepts PKINIT authentication with the matching private key and issues a TGT, from which the NT hash is recovered (UnPAC-the-hash). No password knowledge or reset is needed.
defense.prerequisites: Write over the target's msDS-KeyCredentialLink (GenericWrite/GenericAll/WriteProperty), a PKINIT-capable DC certificate, and a clock in sync with the DC.
defense.impact: Full takeover of the target account (TGT + NT hash) without changing its password, stealthily and reversibly.
defense.detection: [MITRE T1098 / T1558.004] Event 5136 (directory object modified) where AttributeLDAPDisplayName = msDS-KeyCredentialLink on a user/computer object; Event 4768 (AS-REQ) using PKINIT with a certificate on an account that does not normally use smart-card logon; correlate the 5136 write with a subsequent PKINIT TGT for the same principal.
defense.artifacts: 5136 events on msDS-KeyCredentialLink; 4768 PKINIT AS-REQ with Certificate Information populated; certipy/pywhisker exported .pfx on the attacker host.
defense.splunk_spl:
index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=5136 AttributeLDAPDisplayName="msDS-KeyCredentialLink"
| table _time, SubjectUserName, ObjectDN, OperationType

index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=4768 Certificate_Thumbprint=*
| stats count by Account_Name, Client_Address, Certificate_Thumbprint
defense.sentinel_kql:
SecurityEvent
| where EventID == 5136 and AttributeLDAPDisplayName == "msDS-KeyCredentialLink"
| project TimeGenerated, SubjectUserName, ObjectDN, OperationType
| join kind=leftouter (
    SecurityEvent | where EventID == 4768 and isnotempty(CertificateThumbprint)
    | project PkinitTime=TimeGenerated, TargetUserName, IpAddress, CertificateThumbprint
) on $left.ObjectDN == $right.TargetUserName
| sort by TimeGenerated desc
defense.prevention: Audit and tightly scope who can write msDS-KeyCredentialLink (remove unneeded GenericWrite/GenericAll from service accounts and low-privileged principals); enable and monitor Event 5136 on that attribute; deploy Microsoft Defender for Identity (detects Shadow Credentials); prefer tiered admin so write access on Tier-0 objects is minimal.
defense.evasion: certipy shadow auto removes the planted key credential after use; target a single account and clean up to leave only transient 5136/4768 events.
defense.misconfiguration: Low-privileged or service accounts hold GenericWrite/GenericAll (or explicit WriteProperty on msDS-KeyCredentialLink) over other users/computers, usually from over-permissive ACLs or nested group ownership.
defense.vulnerable_config:
# BloodHound shows an AddKeyCredentialLink / GenericWrite / GenericAll edge to the target.
# Confirm the ACL:
Get-DomainObjectAcl -Identity <target_account> -ResolveGUIDs |
  ? { $_.ActiveDirectoryRights -match 'WriteProperty|GenericWrite|GenericAll' }
# Writable msDS-KeyCredentialLink = Shadow Credentials possible.
defense.secure_config:
# Remove the excessive right (example: strip GenericAll from a service account):
# Use dsacls or Set-Acl to remove the ACE granting write over the target object.
dsacls "CN=<target_account>,OU=Users,DC=<domain>" /R "<domain>\<service_account>"

# Monitor the attribute (enable directory-service auditing for object modification),
# then alert on Event 5136 where AttributeLDAPDisplayName == msDS-KeyCredentialLink.

interview.q: What is a Shadow Credentials attack and why is it stealthier than ForceChangePassword?
interview.a: It abuses write access to the target's msDS-KeyCredentialLink attribute to add an attacker-controlled key credential, then uses PKINIT to get a TGT and UnPAC the NT hash. Unlike a forced password reset it does not change the account password - so it does not break services or alert the owner, and it is reversible by removing the added key.

interview.q: As a SOC analyst, what would you monitor to detect Shadow Credentials abuse?
interview.a: Event 5136 (directory object modified) where AttributeLDAPDisplayName = msDS-KeyCredentialLink, correlated with a subsequent Event 4768 PKINIT AS-REQ (certificate logon) for the same principal - especially on accounts that never normally use smart-card auth. Defender for Identity also flags it.

interview.q: What must be true in the environment for this attack to work?
interview.a: You need write over the target's msDS-KeyCredentialLink (GenericWrite/GenericAll/WriteProperty), a DC with a PKINIT-capable certificate (normal with AD CS or default DCs), and a clock in sync with the DC or PKINIT fails with KRB_AP_ERR_SKEW.

explain:
certipy-ad shadow auto automates the whole Shadow Credentials attack:
  -u <user>@<domain> -p <password>  authenticate as the account you already control
  -account <target_account>         the victim whose msDS-KeyCredentialLink you write to
  -dc-ip <dc_ip>                    the Domain Controller to talk to
'shadow auto' adds a key credential, authenticates via PKINIT, UnPACs the NT hash, then removes the key it added (cleanup).
